lead: The Navier–Stokes equations are Newton’s second law written for every small element of a viscous fluid. Pressure, gravity and viscous friction produce the acceleration of the element. The equations are nonlinear, so no general solution exists. A few simple flows can be solved exactly by dropping terms that vanish; these give velocity profiles, maximum and mean speeds, and discharge for flows between plates and in pipes. Engineers use them for lubrication, viscometers, microchannels and as the starting point of computational fluid dynamics.
prereq: You need: Newton’s law of viscosity from Unit 1, the velocity field and continuity from Unit 2, and control-volume momentum from 3.6.

sections.h3: The stress on a small element

blocks.text: Take a small rectangular element of fluid. On each face the surrounding fluid pushes inward with pressure p and also drags along the face with viscous shear stress τ. For a Newtonian fluid τ = μ du/dy in simple shear. The net force is the pressure force −∇p per unit volume plus the viscous force μ∇²V per unit volume, where V is the velocity vector, p is pressure, ρ is density, g is gravitational acceleration and μ is dynamic viscosity. Gravity adds ρg per unit volume.

blocks.where: V = (u, v, w) is the velocity vector in m/s; ρ is density in kg/m³; p is pressure in Pa; g is gravitational acceleration in m/s²; μ is dynamic viscosity in Pa·s. The terms are local acceleration ∂V/∂t, convective acceleration V·∇V, pressure force −∇p, gravity force ρg, and viscous force μ∇²V, all per unit volume.

blocks.text: The left side is mass per unit volume times acceleration. The terms in order are local, convective, pressure, gravity and viscous. The convective term contains products of velocity and velocity gradients. That product makes the equation nonlinear, and nonlinear equations do not have a general formula for all flows. Exact solutions exist only when most terms are zero or constant.

blocks.where: ∇·V is the divergence of velocity in s⁻¹. This is the continuity equation for an incompressible fluid; it states that volume is conserved.

sections.h3: Fully developed flow between parallel plates

blocks.text: Call the flow direction x and the direction across the gap y. The plates are at y = 0 and y = h, both infinite in z, so nothing changes with z. Fully developed means the velocity profile no longer changes with x: ∂u/∂x = 0. Continuity for incompressible flow in two dimensions is ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0. With ∂u/∂x = 0, ∂v/∂y = 0, so v is constant across the gap. At both solid walls v = 0, hence v = 0 everywhere. The flow is parallel to the plates.

For steady, fully developed flow the left side of the Navier–Stokes equation is zero. The x equation reduces to 0 = −dp/dx + μ d²u/dy². Integrate twice and apply no slip. For plane Poiseuille flow, both plates fixed, u(0) = u(h) = 0:

blocks.where: u is velocity in m/s at height y in m; μ is dynamic viscosity in Pa·s; dp/dx is pressure gradient in Pa/m; h is the gap in m.

blocks.text: The maximum is at y = h/2: u_max = (−dp/dx)h²/(8μ). The mean is (2/3)u_max. Discharge per metre width is q = mean × h = (−dp/dx)h³/(12μ). For Couette flow, the upper plate moves at speed U and the pressure gradient is zero. With u(0) = 0 and u(h) = U, u = Uy/h, the mean is U/2, and the shear stress is τ = μU/h. The figure shows both profiles.

sections.h3: Pipe flow and other exact solutions

blocks.text: For a circular pipe of radius R with axis x, fully developed laminar flow gives the Hagen–Poiseuille profile u(r) = (1/(4μ))(−dp/dx)(R² − r²). The maximum is at the centre, u_max = (−dp/dx)R²/(4μ), and the mean is half the maximum. The discharge is Q = πR⁴(−dp/dx)/(8μ). The derivation and pipe losses are in Unit 4.

blocks.where: u(r) is velocity in m/s at radius r in m; R is pipe radius in m; μ is dynamic viscosity in Pa·s; dp/dx is pressure gradient in Pa/m.

blocks.text: Stokes flow past a small sphere gives drag F = 6πμRU for very slow flow, where U is the sphere speed and R its radius; it is one exact solution of the full equations with the convective term neglected. These solutions are used in viscometers, lubrication films and microfluidic channels. They are exact only for laminar, fully developed, simple geometry flows; they are not a general answer for a pump, a valve or a car body.

figure.caption: Velocity profiles between parallel plates: the parabola is pressure-driven Poiseuille flow with its peak at mid-gap; the straight line is Couette flow driven by the moving upper plate.

spec.aria: A graph of velocity profiles between parallel plates: a parabola for pressure-driven flow with its peak at mid-gap, and a straight line for flow driven by a moving upper plate.

examples.question: Oil of dynamic viscosity 0.05 Pa·s flows steadily and fully developed between two fixed parallel plates 5 mm apart. The pressure falls by 1200 Pa per metre in the flow direction and the flow is laminar. Find the maximum velocity, the mean velocity and the discharge per metre width.
steps: List the data: h = 5 mm = 5 × 10⁻³ m, μ = 0.05 Pa·s, and the pressure drop per metre is −dp/dx = 1200 Pa/m because pressure falls in the flow direction.
For plane Poiseuille flow the maximum velocity is u_max = (−dp/dx)h²/(8μ).
For this parabolic profile the mean is two-thirds of the maximum: mean = (2/3) × 0.075 = 0.05 m/s.
Discharge per metre width is q = mean × h = 0.05 × 5 × 10⁻³ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m²/s per metre width.
examples.answer: u_max = 0.075 m/s, mean velocity = 0.05 m/s and discharge = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m²/s per metre width.

traps: Dropping terms without saying why: for fully developed flow ∂u/∂x = 0 and v = 0; for Couette flow dp/dx = 0; for Stokes flow the convective term is neglected because the Reynolds number is very small.
Losing the sign: for flow in the +x direction, pressure decreases, so dp/dx is negative. Use (−dp/dx) as a positive driving quantity.
Mixing maximum and mean: between fixed plates the mean is (2/3)u_max; in a circular pipe the mean is (1/2)u_max.
Using an exact solution outside its assumptions: laminar, fully developed, constant μ, simple geometry. A pipe entrance, a valve or a pump is not covered.
Writing Euler instead of Navier–Stokes: Euler has no viscous term and applies to inviscid flow; Navier–Stokes keeps μ∇²V.

quiz.q: Write the incompressible Navier–Stokes equation in vector form and name the five terms.
quiz.a: ρ(∂V/∂t + V·∇V) = −∇p + ρg + μ∇²V, with ∇·V = 0. Terms: local acceleration, convective acceleration, pressure force, gravity force and viscous force per unit volume.

quiz.q: Why is the Navier–Stokes equation nonlinear, and what practical consequence does that have?
quiz.a: The convective acceleration V·∇V contains products of velocity components and their gradients. Because of this product, solutions cannot be superposed in general and no general closed-form solution exists for arbitrary geometry and boundary conditions.

quiz.q: For steady, fully developed flow between two fixed parallel plates, show that the transverse velocity v is zero.
quiz.a: Continuity gives ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0. Fully developed means ∂u/∂x = 0, so ∂v/∂y = 0 and v depends only on x. At the impermeable walls v = 0; hence v = 0 everywhere.

quiz.q: Oil of viscosity 0.2 Pa·s fills a 2 mm gap between a fixed lower plate and an upper plate moving at 0.6 m/s. Assume plane Couette flow. Find the velocity at 0.8 mm above the lower plate and the shear stress on the moving plate.
In plane Poiseuille flow the gap is 4 mm, μ = 0.02 Pa·s, and the pressure drop is 800 Pa per metre. Find u_max and the discharge per metre width.
For plane Poiseuille flow at fixed pressure gradient and viscosity, the gap h is doubled. By what factors do u_max and discharge per metre width change?
quiz.a: u_max ∝ h², so it becomes 4 times larger. Discharge per metre width ∝ h³, so it becomes 8 times larger.

quiz.q: A student uses dp/dx = +1200 Pa/m in u = (1/(2μ))(−dp/dx)(hy − y²) and obtains negative velocities. What sign convention was missed?
quiz.a: For flow in the +x direction pressure must fall, so dp/dx = −1200 Pa/m. The formula already contains (−dp/dx); substituting +1200 makes the driving term negative. Use the magnitude 1200 Pa/m as −dp/dx.

quiz.q: State the Hagen–Poiseuille result for laminar flow in a circular pipe of radius R, and give the mean velocity in terms of the maximum.
quiz.a: u(r) = (1/(4μ))(−dp/dx)(R² − r²), u_max = (−dp/dx)R²/(4μ), Q = πR⁴(−dp/dx)/(8μ), and mean velocity = u_max/2.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the same equations are solved numerically in CFD codes, with turbulence models such as RANS or LES because direct solution of every eddy is too costly. Lubrication theory uses the same reduction to thin films, and microfluidic devices often sit in the Stokes-flow limit where the convective term is negligible. Search for “Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness”, “RANS equations” and “Stokes flow” to go further.
